why: The options form an even 0.4 grid: 0.1 comes from reading Territory I's bar for J (1.67 − 1.55) and 1.3 from taking J's Spend per customer series (3.02 − 1.67 ≈ 1.35), so 0.9 continues the spacing; capping A at 100% gives 0.3, not 0.5.

The options are the four prices tested; the slips that still pick €0.07 (stationery sales taken as profit, the market's 10% margin) are both named in sourceHas, while ignoring stationery moves the answer to €0.08.

A reverses the sign, D charges the extra 30c on all 600,000 wraps (ignoring the tier and the 10% volume rise), and C counts the 60,000 extra wraps at $3.00 (using $4.00 throughout and forgetting the $2.50 handling cost); ignoring the tier or the volume alone gives −$168k or −$144k, not the answer.

D (43%) leaves public buildings out of buildings (8.4 ÷ 19.7), and A and B are near misses (27.4% and 4.6%) that look right if the 19.7 total is rounded to 18 or 20; dividing cars by the total instead (21%) makes C false.

A, B and D are true but look false after a common slip (using cumulative percentages instead of each group's step, or leaving out the £2.7m variable cost), and no slip leaves C as the only false statement.

The options form a tight $30 grid (about 6% of the answer), so neighbours are where rough estimates land; swapping the two percentages, using 2013 as the base or taking the wrong tiers gives $435 to $475, not $516.
A ranks by profit lost alone, B ranks by probability alone, and C swaps the close pair N ($0.7m) and M ($0.6m), which happens if M's unlabelled $3m is read half a gridline high.
14 and 21 come from reading the wrong row ('have considered' and 'send now or before'), and 33 continues their steady ratio of about 1.5; the relative gap (12%) lands on 14, not 9.

1.2 reads the antivirus series, 3.8 reads it and forgets to average (3.7), and 1.6 forgets to average and reads the unlabelled $1,950m as $2,000m (1.65); the period-counting slips that sourceHas names give 0.28 to 0.37, more than 20% from 0.5.
B ranks by cost alone, C ranks by probability alone, and D puts ground staff above engineers, which happens if G's unlabelled $1m is read half a gridline high as $2m.
